query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In a single‐phase, compositionally complex high-entropy alloy, brittle behavior emerges not from classical grain-boundary segregation or intermetallic precipitation but from a thermally and mechanically induced transition of the grain-boundary morphology from an initially serrated (strain‐distributing) state to a straighter form that cannot effectively arrest local strain concentrations.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase high-entropy alloy with fine, serrated grain boundaries that distribute strain evenly and maintain high ductility.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to controlled high-temperature thermal cycling combined with mechanical loading representative of service conditions.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperatures (e.g., near 650°C as used in prior studies) and applied strain rates typical of operating conditions in high-temperature applications, ensuring that the only variable is the induced change in grain-boundary morphology.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain-boundary morphology (specifically the transition from serrated boundaries to straight boundaries).
generation.mechanism: Under service conditions, thermal activation permits local precipitate coarsening or redistribution of atomic species even in a single-phase alloy. This change interferes with the stability of the serrated grain-boundary configuration, causing a transition to straight boundaries. Unlike conventional alloys where embrittlement is tied to grain-boundary segregation, here the loss of serration reduces the ability to distribute strain, leading to localized stress, intergranular cracking, and thus brittle behavior.
generation.predicted_outcome: After thermal–mechanical cycling, the alloy will exhibit a marked drop in ductility and toughness due to a significant reduction in boundary serration, with mechanical tests revealing lower tensile fracture strains and reduced creep rupture life relative to the baseline state.
generation.baseline: The as-processed single-phase high-entropy alloy with serrated grain boundaries and uniform strain distribution, demonstrating high toughness and ductility.
generation.boundary: This mechanistic behavior is expected to manifest under high-temperature, high-strain conditions typical of demanding service environments; at lower temperatures the serrated morphology—and hence the toughness—should persist.
generation.uncertainty: The precise thermal or microstructural conditions (e.g., critical temperature and exposure duration) that drive the morphological transition remain to be fully elucidated, and it is uncertain whether additional microstructural transformations may concurrently contribute to embrittlement.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of identical single-phase high-entropy alloy samples with confirmed serrated grain boundaries. Subject one set to repeated high-temperature thermal and mechanical cycling expected to induce a transition in grain-boundary morphology, while maintaining the other set under baseline (lower-temperature or stress-free) conditions. Post-exposure, use high-resolution electron microscopy to examine grain-boundary morphology and perform tensile and creep tests to assess mechanical properties.
measurements: Tensile fracture strain and ductility measurements
In situ strain field mapping (e.g., digital image correlation)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermally and mechanically cycled samples do not exhibit a change from serrated to predominantly straight grain boundaries, or if no significant reduction in ductility and creep life is observed relative to the baseline samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

## Abstract
ABSTRACTIn this study, tensile and creep deformation of a high-entropy alloy processed by selective laser melting (SLM) has been investigated; hot ductility drop was identified at first, and the loss of ductility at elevated temperature was associated with intergranular fracture. By modifying the grain boundary morphology from straight to serration, the hot ductility drop issue has been resolved successfully. The serrated grain boundary could be achieved by reducing the cooling rate of solution heat treatment, which allowed the coarsening of L12 structured γ′ precipitates to interfere with mobile grain boundaries, resulting in undulation of the grain boundary morphology. Tensile and creep tests at 650°C were conducted, and serrated grain boundary could render a significant increase in tensile fracture strain and creep rupture life by a factor of 3.5 and 400, respectively. Detailed microstructure analysis has indicated that serrated grain boundary could distribute strains more evenly than that of straight morphology.
